options.content:
### Daily Brief — what this dashboard answers

Every panel here drives a decision. They are grouped by question, most urgent first: **is it working**, **are people using it**, **are the briefs good enough**, **which features earn their place**, and **how does it perform**.

**Reading rules.** Titles name the statistic and the window. Panels marked *(now)* or *(all time)* are levels and ignore the time picker on purpose — their descriptions say why. Everything else re-scopes to the range you pick. Every average names its denominator. A blank panel means the answer is *undefined* for that range, not zero — where a window has no events to divide by, the line breaks rather than dropping to a misleading zero.

**Filter by org.** The **Org** control scopes every database-backed panel — readers, delivery, acceptance, custom prompts — to one or more organisations. This matters more than it looks: the brief agent is configurable per org (`organization.dailyBriefAgentSlug`), so a quality number blended across orgs is averaging the output of *different agents*, and a single wholly-broken tenant can vanish into a healthy fleet-wide average. Panels reading the metrics store cannot be scoped this way — the store carries no org label — and each one says so in its description.

**Start dates, honestly.** Brief *deliveries* go back to the feature's first brief (2026-07-09). Per-user *activity* — reads, regenerations, history browsing — starts **2026-08-20**. Opt-in/opt-out *events* and the subscriber gauge start when the toggle shipped (2026-08-20). Selecting a range that reaches further back shows blanks for those panels: that is missing history, not zero usage. Nothing has been back-filled or inferred.

**Two data sources.** Delivery, reader and prompt panels read the application's own Postgres, so their counts are exact rather than sampled. Rate, quality and performance panels read the metrics store. One panel mixes both and says so.

**Small numbers are still small.** Distributions and per-user averages need a real population before they mean anything; treat single-digit readings as directional only.

panels.title: Subscribers with no brief today (now)
panels.description:
IGNORES THE TIME PICKER - it is a live check on this morning.

How many people have Morning Brief switched on but have no finished brief for today. This is the feature's worst failure mode made visible: the user opens the app, there is nothing there, and no error is shown to anyone.

GOOD: 0.
BAD: anything above 0 after the morning fan-out has drained. Each unit is one person who was promised a brief and did not get one.

Expect a non-zero reading while the cron is still running; that is the fan-out in progress, not a fault.

defaults.noValue: no subscribers

targets.rawSql: SELECT count(*) AS "no brief today" FROM users u WHERE u."orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND u."dailyBriefEnabled" AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM generated_content g WHERE g."userId"=u.id AND g.kind='DAILY_BRIEF' AND g."dateBucket"=to_char(now() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD') AND g."generatedAt" IS NOT NULL)

panels.title: Delivery completeness (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Perfect delivery = every subscriber gets a brief every day, so the ideal is (subscribers x days). This is the share of that ideal actually delivered.

GOOD: 100%.
BAD: 60% means four mornings in ten produced nothing for the average subscriber.

Reads generated_content, so it has FULL HISTORY back to the feature's first brief. The day count is clamped to days the feature existed, so a range reaching back before that does not manufacture a shortfall.

CAVEAT: subscriber count is a live reading while the numerator spans the range, so a burst of recent sign-ups drags it down for a while - those people were not subscribers for the whole range.

defaults.noValue: no deliveries in this range

targets.rawSql: SELECT count(*)::float / NULLIF((SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE "dailyBriefEnabled" AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring})) * GREATEST((to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD')::date - GREATEST(to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD')::date, (SELECT min("dateBucket")::date FROM generated_content WHERE kind='DAILY_BRIEF' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring})))) + 1, 1),0) AS "delivery completeness" FROM generated_content WHERE kind='DAILY_BRIEF' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "generatedAt" IS NOT NULL AND $__timeFilter("generatedAt")

panels.title: Scheduled briefs delivered late (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Share of the scheduled briefs that DID arrive but arrived more than 30 minutes after the time the cron was aiming for. It exists, just not when it was needed.

GOOD: flat at zero.
BAD: any sustained level, and especially a rise that tracks subscriber growth - that is the morning fan-out queueing behind the shared model-throughput limit, so the users at the back of the queue get their brief hours late.

30 minutes is used because it is a real bucket edge in the underlying histogram; a threshold that is not a bucket boundary returns a silently wrong answer.

COUNTS ONLY BRIEFS THAT SUCCEEDED. A brief that never arrived at all is not late, it is missing - see 'Generation failure rate by trigger' in the Generation reliability row below. Read the two together: a pipeline that fails almost everything and delivers one brief on time scores a perfect zero here.

The failure line that used to share this panel now lives in that row, split by trigger, because scheduled and user-triggered failures are different problems and were being averaged together.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: no scheduled runs in this range

panels.title: Opt-in rate: subscribers / all accounts (now)
panels.description:
THE BIG NUMBER IS RIGHT NOW; the sparkline shows the selected range.

Share of all accounts with Morning Brief switched on. Fixed denominator (everyone who could switch it on), so it stays comparable as the company grows.

GOOD: rising, or high and steady.
BAD: flat while headcount grows - the feature is not spreading, it is being carried by early adopters. A step DOWN is somebody deliberately switching it off.

Deliberately not a time-average: averaging a ratio weights every scrape equally regardless of how many accounts existed at that instant, and would report ~49% for a population that was 50% and is now 0%.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: no scrape data in this range

panels.title: Distinct readers (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Exact count of different people who opened a brief in the range - COUNT(DISTINCT userId) from the application's own table, not an estimate.

Set the range to 7 days for weekly actives, 30 for monthly. Unlike an all-time total this CAN GO DOWN, which is the point.

GOOD: growing, or tracking the subscriber count.
BAD: falling while opt-ins rise - people are signing up and not reading.

Per-user activity has been recorded since 2026-08-20; ranges reaching further back read blank rather than zero, which is missing history and not a drop in usage.

defaults.noValue: no reader activity in this range

targets.rawSql: SELECT count(DISTINCT "userId") AS readers FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='view' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD')

panels.title: People switching Morning Brief on and off (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Gross flow in each direction - the churn the subscriber level cannot show.

Ten people switching on and ten switching off leaves the level perfectly flat and reads as 'nothing is happening', when in fact the feature is replacing its entire audience.

GOOD: the ON bar clearly taller than OFF.
BAD: the two bars similar - you are acquiring and losing at the same rate, so growth is a treadmill.
WORST: OFF taller than ON. Check the date against the failure and rejection panels below to see whether quality caused it.

Counts real transitions only: re-saving the same value does not count, verified against the live route. Counts EVENTS, so somebody who leaves and returns appears in both bars - deliberately, because that is a different story from never leaving.

Opt-in events are recorded from the moment the toggle shipped.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: no toggle activity in this range

panels.title: Distinct readers per day (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. One point per calendar day, each an exact count of the different people who opened a brief that day, plotted against the number of subscribers those readers are drawn from.

THE SOLID LINE IS THE MEASUREMENT: distinct readers per day, COUNT(DISTINCT userId) from the application's own table.

THE DASHED LINE IS CONTEXT, NOT A SECOND METRIC: how many people had Morning Brief switched on at that moment. It is the ceiling the reader count is competing against, and it comes from a different source - a gauge re-read from the database every 60s - so it moves continuously while the reader line steps once per day. Do not read the two as equally weighted series.

READ THE GAP. A flat reader line means completely different things at 5 subscribers and at 500. If the lines sit close together, almost everyone who subscribed is reading. A widening gap is the number to worry about: subscribers accumulating who never open anything, each costing a full agent run every morning.

GOOD: the solid line tracking the dashed one as both rise.
BAD: the dashed line climbing while the solid one stays flat - you are adding subscribers, not readers.

DO NOT ADD THE READER POINTS TOGETHER. These are people-per-day: somebody who reads on ten days appears once on each of ten points, so summing gives user-days and counts them ten times. For a de-duplicated total across the range, read the 'Distinct readers (selected range)' tile above - it does the de-duplication properly and is not derivable from this chart.

START DATES DIFFER AND NEITHER LINE IS BACK-FILLED. Per-user activity has been recorded since 2026-08-20 and the subscriber gauge since 2026-08-20 21:52. Before those points each line simply stops rather than drawing a zero, so a short dashed line means 'not measured yet', never 'nobody subscribed'.

ONLY THE SOLID LINE OBEYS THE ORG FILTER. The reader count comes from the database and is scoped to the Org selection; the dashed subscriber reference comes from the metrics store, which has no org label, so it always shows every organisation. WITH AN ORG SELECTED THE GAP BETWEEN THE TWO LINES IS MEANINGLESS - you would be comparing one org's readers against every org's subscribers. Read the gap only with Org set to All.

defaults.noValue: no reader activity in this range

targets.rawSql: SELECT "dateBucket"::date AS time, count(DISTINCT "userId") AS "distinct readers" FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='view' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Subscribers and total accounts over time
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. The two levels behind the opt-in rate: how many people have Morning Brief on, and how many accounts exist to switch it on.

This is the diagnostic for the rate tile. A falling rate means either the top line fell or the bottom one rose, and those need opposite responses - this panel says which happened.

GOOD: both rising together.
BAD: accounts rising while subscribers stays flat - new joiners are not finding or not wanting the feature, a discovery problem rather than a quality one.

A LEVEL, so ten people joining and ten leaving draws a flat line. The panel beside it separates those.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: no scrape data in this range

panels.title: How many days each reader showed up (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. The distribution behind every average on this page - is usage broad, or carried by a handful of people?

An average cannot tell a population where everyone shows up sometimes from one where two people show up constantly and the rest came once. This can.

GOOD: weight in the right-hand buckets - people who find the brief keep coming back.
BAD: a tall '1 day' bar - most readers tried it once and never returned, and every per-user average is being propped up by a small committed minority.

Buckets count PEOPLE and sum to the total distinct readers, so this one can be read as a share of the whole.

Per-user activity has been recorded since 2026-08-20; ranges reaching further back read blank rather than zero, which is missing history and not a drop in usage.

defaults.noValue: no reader activity in this range

targets.rawSql: WITH per_user AS (SELECT "userId", count(DISTINCT "dateBucket") AS days FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='view' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') GROUP BY 1) SELECT CASE WHEN days=1 THEN '1 day' WHEN days<=3 THEN '2-3 days' WHEN days<=7 THEN '4-7 days' WHEN days<=20 THEN '8-20 days' ELSE '21+ days' END AS "days active", count(*) AS readers FROM per_user GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY min(days)

panels.title: Kept as-is: share of read brief-days never regenerated (${smoothing}-day window)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Of the brief-days somebody actually opened, the share they left alone - no regeneration at any point that day - tracked over time so you can see it MOVE after a prompt, model or response change ships.

ONE DOT PER DAY BY DEFAULT. The 'Acceptance smoothing' control at the top of the dashboard sets how many days each point pools. It starts at 1, meaning every dot is that day on its own with no pooling at all - so a change you ship shows up as a SHARP STEP on the day it landed, which is what you want when correlating acceptance with a release.

WIDEN IT WHEN THE DAILY LINE IS TOO NOISY TO READ. On a small or quiet population a single person's single decision can swing a day between 0% and 100%; pooling 3, 7 or 14 days averages that out and shows the level instead. The cost is responsiveness: at any setting above 1 a step change becomes a RAMP that begins on the day of the change and finishes that many days later, so align a release with where the ramp STARTS, not where it ends. At 1 there is no ramp.

The sample-size bars are pooled over the same window, so they always show the exact denominator behind the point above them whatever setting you pick.

THE BARS ARE THE SAMPLE SIZE, not a second metric - how many read brief-days went into that point, on the right axis. A point at 100% off one reading and a point at 100% off forty look identical without them. Ignore the line wherever the bars are short.

THE DENOMINATOR IS DELIBERATELY RESTRICTED TO BRIEFS THAT WERE READ. Somebody who never opened their brief also never regenerated it, and counting that as approval would fill the number with indifference. Only a person who saw the brief and chose to keep it is evidence of quality.

GOOD: a high, flat line on tall bars - people open the brief and it is good enough as delivered.
BAD: a sustained fall on steady bars - people are looking at the brief and rejecting what they see, the sharpest dissatisfaction signal on this dashboard.
NOT BAD: the line vanishing. A gap means nobody read a brief in that window, which is not 0% acceptance - it is no data, and no point is drawn.

HISTORY IS SHORT, AND THE PANEL CLAMPS ITSELF. Read and regeneration records begin 2026-08-20. Because a brief-day only enters the denominator when a read was recorded for it, every earlier day drops out automatically rather than counting as a silent acceptance - widening the range cannot inflate this with fiction. At the time of writing 31 brief-days exist but only 2 were read, so expect a short line on very short bars.

TODAY IS EXCLUDED. A brief delivered this morning has not had a full day to be rejected, so including it would inflate acceptance every morning and sag through the day.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM 'First-try acceptance rate' BESIDE IT: that one is a ratio of EVENTS from the metrics store - regenerations divided by briefs delivered - with months of history but no idea who read what. This one is a proportion of USER-DAYS from the database, exact but only since 2026-08-20. They measure different things and will not agree; neither is wrong.

ONE KNOWN IMPRECISION: a read is recorded against the day the screen was opened, not against the brief that was displayed, so somebody who opened the screen and immediately browsed to an older brief still counts as having read that day's brief.

WHAT COUNTS AS A REJECTION CHANGED, AND THE HISTORY WAS RESET. This panel used to treat ANY regeneration that day as a rejection, which wrongly counted somebody retrying after a failed brief as dissatisfied. It now only counts regenerations whose origin was 'replacing the scheduled brief' or 'replacing my own re-run'; retries after a failure and first-brief-of-day creations are ignored.

The origin of past regenerations could not be recovered, so those rows were DELETED on 2026-08-24 rather than left asserting acceptance they cannot evidence. Consequence: until new regenerations accumulate, every read brief-day has no rejection against it and THIS PANEL WILL READ 100%. That is absence of data, not perfect quality. Trust it only once the sample-size bars are tall enough to have contained a rejection.

A BRIEF CAN ONLY BE REJECTED ON ITS OWN DAY. Regenerate always targets today's brief - the route takes no date - so somebody who opens Monday's brief on Wednesday and dislikes it cannot re-run it; pressing the button regenerates Wednesday's brief instead. Both sides of this ratio are locked to the same day, so the measure stays internally consistent, but two edges follow: a brief-day nobody opened on its own day never enters the denominator at all, and dissatisfaction with an older brief is recorded against today's brief rather than the one that caused it.

defaults.noValue: no brief was both delivered and read in this range

targets.rawSql: WITH bounds AS ( SELECT to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD')::date AS d0, LEAST(to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD')::date, (to_char(now() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata','YYYY-MM-DD')::date - 1)) AS d1 ), read_days AS ( SELECT DISTINCT g."userId", g."dateBucket"::date AS d, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM daily_brief_activity r WHERE r."userId"=g."userId" AND r."dateBucket"=g."dateBucket" AND r.kind='regenerate' AND r."rejectionCount" > 0) AS rejected FROM generated_content g JOIN daily_brief_activity v ON v."userId"=g."userId" AND v."dateBucket"=g."dateBucket" AND v.kind='view' WHERE g.kind='DAILY_BRIEF' AND g."orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND g."generatedAt" IS NOT NULL AND g."dateBucket"::date <= (SELECT d1 FROM bounds) AND g."dateBucket"::date >= (SELECT d0 FROM bounds) - (${smoothing}::int - 1) ), cal AS ( SELECT generate_series((SELECT d0 FROM bounds),(SELECT d1 FROM bounds),'1 day')::date AS day ) SELECT c.day AS time, (SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT rd.rejected)::float / NULLIF(count(*),0) FROM read_days rd WHERE rd.d BETWEEN c.day - (${smoothing}::int - 1) AND c.day) AS "kept as-is", (SELECT count(*) FROM read_days rd2 WHERE rd2.d BETWEEN c.day - (${smoothing}::int - 1) AND c.day) AS "read brief-days in window" FROM cal c ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Why people regenerate (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. What the Regenerate button is actually being used for. This is the panel that stops 'regenerations are up' being misreported as either engagement or dissatisfaction.

replacing_scheduled_brief - the morning brief was rejected. A QUALITY problem.
replacing_own_regeneration - their own re-run was rejected too. A WORSE quality problem.
retry_after_failure - the previous run errored. A RELIABILITY problem; it says nothing about quality.
first_brief_of_day - no brief existed yet. Not dissatisfaction at all, just normal use.

GOOD: dominated by first_brief_of_day with a thin retry bar.
BAD: a fat retry_after_failure bar - while that is wide, regeneration volume is mostly measuring outages and must not be reported as unhappiness.

Filtered to the four defined origins: a fifth value from a superseded build still sits in the metrics store and would otherwise appear as a phantom bar.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: no regenerations in this range

panels.title: Share of readers who used each feature (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Of the people who opened a brief in the range, the share who also used each feature at least once.

THIS IS THE PANEL FOR CUT DECISIONS. A feature sitting near zero across a long range is one almost nobody touches, and is a candidate for removal. Counts PEOPLE, so one enthusiast cannot make a dead feature look alive.

GOOD: a feature you invested in sitting high.
BAD: near zero over 30 days - either nobody wants it, or nobody can find it. Those need opposite responses, so check discoverability before deleting anything.

Cannot exceed 100%: you have to open a brief to be counted. Note that 'browsed history' covers both the recent list and the calendar; the panel below splits those.

Per-user activity has been recorded since 2026-08-20; ranges reaching further back read blank rather than zero, which is missing history and not a drop in usage.

THE 'REGENERATED A BRIEF' BAR IS RESET AND WILL READ ZERO. Regeneration rows were deleted on 2026-08-24 when rejection tracking was added, so this bar counts only regenerations since then. Zero here means 'not recorded yet', NOT 'nobody uses Regenerate' - the metrics store shows regenerations continuing throughout. Do not make a cut decision about Regenerate from this bar until it has had time to refill; use 'Why people regenerate' in the quality row, which kept its full history.

defaults.noValue: no reader activity in this range

targets.rawSql: WITH v AS (SELECT count(DISTINCT "userId") n FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='view' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD')) SELECT 'regenerated a brief' AS feature, (SELECT count(DISTINCT "userId") FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='regenerate' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD'))::float / NULLIF((SELECT n FROM v),0) AS share UNION ALL SELECT 'browsed brief history', (SELECT count(DISTINCT "userId") FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE kind='switch' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD'))::float / NULLIF((SELECT n FROM v),0)

panels.title: People who used each way of reaching an older brief (all time)
panels.description:
IGNORES THE TIME PICKER - these are lifetime distinct-user counts held as Redis sets, which carry no dates.

The recent list and the calendar are two different controls for the same job. The calendar is the ONLY way to reach a brief older than the handful shown in the list, so its bar is the direct read on whether anyone wants older briefs.

GOOD: both bars healthy - the history feature is genuinely used.
BAD: the calendar bar near zero over the feature's whole life - it is an expensive control nobody needs, and a clean deletion candidate.

THE SETS OVERLAP: somebody who used both is counted in both, so the bars do not sum to the reader count and must never be drawn as a pie.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

defaults.noValue: nobody has browsed history yet

panels.title: Custom instructions: how far people get (now)
panels.description:
IGNORES THE TIME PICKER - a live funnel read from the database.

Three steps: how many people subscribe, how many wrote custom instructions for their brief, and how many still have those instructions switched on.

GOOD: a healthy share of subscribers writing instructions, and almost all of them keeping them enabled.
BAD: a tall drop from 'subscribers' to 'wrote instructions' - the feature is undiscovered or too much effort.
WORST: people writing instructions and then switching them OFF. That is a considered rejection - they tried steering the brief and decided it made things worse.

Instructions are stored per user per agent and kept when disabled rather than deleted, so the gap between the last two bars is real abandonment rather than tidying up.

defaults.noValue: no subscribers yet

targets.rawSql: SELECT 'subscribers' AS step, (SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE "dailyBriefEnabled" AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring})) AS people UNION ALL SELECT 'wrote instructions', (SELECT count(*) FROM user_agent_instructions WHERE "agentSlug"='daily-brief' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND length(trim(instructions))>0) UNION ALL SELECT 'kept them enabled', (SELECT count(*) FROM user_agent_instructions WHERE "agentSlug"='daily-brief' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND length(trim(instructions))>0 AND enabled)

panels.title: Do custom instructions reduce regeneration? (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Readers split by whether they have custom instructions switched on, and how many times each group re-ran their brief per person.

THE QUESTION THIS SETTLES: do custom prompts actually make briefs better, or do they just change the wording? Regeneration is the dissatisfaction proxy, so if instructions work, the left bar should be LOWER.

GOOD: the 'has custom instructions' bar clearly lower - people who steer the brief are happier with it, which argues for surfacing the feature harder.
BAD: equal bars - instructions change the output without changing satisfaction.
WORST: instructions HIGHER - people who write prompts are the fussy ones and the brief is not meeting them, or the instructions are actively making it worse.

NOT A CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT: people who write instructions chose to, so they may simply be more demanding users. Treat a difference as a prompt worth investigating, not proof. Both bars need a reasonable number of readers before the comparison means anything - the reader count is shown on each bar.

Per-user activity has been recorded since 2026-08-20; ranges reaching further back read blank rather than zero, which is missing history and not a drop in usage.

BOTH BARS ARE RESET AND WILL READ ZERO. This panel counts regenerations from the activity table, and those rows were deleted on 2026-08-24 when rejection tracking was added. Until new regenerations accumulate, both cohorts show zero and the comparison is empty - which is not evidence that custom instructions make no difference, it is evidence of no data. The panel becomes meaningful again once both cohorts have a reasonable number of readers AND some regenerations.

defaults.noValue: no reader activity in this range

targets.rawSql: WITH ins AS (SELECT DISTINCT "userId" FROM user_agent_instructions WHERE "agentSlug"='daily-brief' AND "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND enabled AND length(trim(instructions))>0), r AS (SELECT "userId", SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE kind='regenerate') AS regens FROM daily_brief_activity WHERE "orgId" IN (${org:sqlstring}) AND "dateBucket" >= to_char($__timeFrom() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND "dateBucket" <= to_char($__timeTo() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AND kind IN ('view','regenerate') GROUP BY 1) SELECT CASE WHEN i."userId" IS NOT NULL THEN 'has custom instructions' ELSE 'no custom instructions' END AS cohort, COALESCE(SUM(regens),0)::float / NULLIF(count(*),0) AS "regenerations per reader", count(*) AS readers FROM r LEFT JOIN ins i ON i."userId"=r."userId" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

panels.title: How long a brief takes vs how long people wait (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. All four lines are SECONDS, so they can be read against each other directly. This is the panel that says whether the wait is survivable.

THE COMPARISON THAT MATTERS: if 'half of leavers had gone by' sits BELOW 'half of briefs took', people are giving up before the brief could possibly arrive - and no amount of quality work will help, because they never see it. The fix is a progress indicator, a notification when it is ready, or a faster pipeline.

GOOD: the patience lines sitting above the generation lines.
BAD: patience below generation - every regeneration is a race the user is losing.

THE PATIENCE LINES ARE A LOWER BOUND AND CLIENT-MEASURED. They come from the browser, count devices rather than people, and are recorded when the screen unmounts - so a closed tab, the very thing being measured, may never report. They also fire on in-app navigation, and the screen sends no cancel signal, so 'left the screen' does not mean 'the run stopped'. Treat them as 'people stopped watching', not 'people cancelled'.

The browser export path is healthy, but these two lines only move when somebody actually walks away mid-regeneration - so long flat stretches are real quiet, not a broken pipe.

NOT AFFECTED BY THE ORG FILTER. This panel reads the metrics store, which carries no org label, so it always shows every organisation regardless of the Org selection at the top. With an org selected, read it as fleet-wide background rather than that org's number.

panels.title: Generation time vs load, and whether failures are timeouts (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Left axis seconds, right axis briefs completed per hour.

TWO QUESTIONS IN ONE CHART.

CAPACITY - can this feature take more users without getting worse for the ones it has? If the slowest-5% line climbs whenever throughput climbs, the pipeline is contended and every new subscriber makes everybody else's brief later. Flat while throughput grows means there is headroom and growth is safe. Rising while throughput is FLAT is a regression in the run itself - a slower model, slower tools, more data per user - and adding capacity will not fix it.

TIMEOUTS - the 'failed runs' line is how long runs took before giving up. When it pins to the top of the histogram it means failures are timeouts rather than errors, which is the mechanism behind the failure rate in 'Scheduled brief problems'. If the two rise together, the cause is duration, and the fix is making generation faster or raising the limit - not retry logic.

GOOD: successful-run line flat and well below the failed-run line; throughput free to grow.
BAD: the successful line creeping up toward the failed line - runs are approaching the ceiling and will start tipping over into failures.

panels.title: Generation failure rate by trigger (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. The share of brief generation runs that ended without producing a brief, split by who asked for the run. Both lines are BAD WHEN HIGH.

THE SPLIT IS THE POINT - these are different product problems:
SCHEDULED - the cron ran and produced nothing. The user wakes up to an empty screen, is shown no error, and may never learn a brief was even attempted. Silent, and the worst outcome the feature has.
USER-TRIGGERED - somebody pressed Regenerate and watched it fail. Visible and annoying, but they know it happened and can press the button again.

GOOD: both flat at zero.
BAD: the SCHEDULED line above a few percent - each point is a morning somebody got nothing and was not told.
ALSO BAD, DIFFERENTLY: the user-triggered line high - the on-demand path is unreliable, which is more visible but more recoverable.

READ THE TWO LINES TOGETHER TO LOCATE THE FAULT. Both rising means something shared broke - the model provider, a tool, a deploy. Only one rising points at that path specifically.

Gaps are honest: where no run of that kind happened in a window the ratio is undefined and the line breaks rather than dropping to a fake zero.

Both counters reset when the backend restarts, and increase() extrapolates to the window edges, so treat these as close estimates rather than exact tallies - a value of 4.7 failures means about five.

panels.title: Failures nobody retried (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Of the generation runs that failed, the share that were never followed by another attempt that day - so the user simply ended the day with nothing.

THIS IS THE HARM METRIC. Every other failure number counts runs; this one counts people left empty-handed. A failure that the user retried into a working brief cost them a wait. A failure nobody retried cost them the feature that day.

GOOD: near zero - failures happen but people recover from them.
BAD: high - failures are terminal. That usually means the failure was SILENT (the scheduled run failed and nobody was told) rather than that people chose to give up, so pair this with the scheduled line in the panel beside it.

THE BARS ARE THE ABSOLUTE COUNT on the right axis; the line is the share. A share off two failures is not a finding - ignore the line where the bars are short.

HOW IT IS DERIVED: every retry-after-failure follows exactly one failed run, one-to-one, so failures minus retries is the number of failures with no follow-up. Recovery can only happen on the day of the failure - Regenerate always targets today's brief - so a next-day attempt is a new day's first attempt, not a recovery, and is correctly excluded.

IT COUNTS RETRY ATTEMPTS, NOT RECOVERIES. A retry can itself fail, so this understates the harm: the true number of people who ended up with nothing is at least this. For whether the retries worked, see 'Attempts until a regeneration succeeds' below.

NOT SPLIT BY TRIGGER, AND IT CANNOT BE. The retry counter carries no trigger label - a retry is always a user regeneration by definition - while the failure it follows may have been scheduled or user-triggered. Subtracting an unsplit number from a split one would be arithmetic nonsense, so this stays aggregate.

Both counters reset when the backend restarts, and increase() extrapolates to the window edges, so treat these as close estimates rather than exact tallies - a value of 4.7 failures means about five.

panels.title: Attempts until a regeneration succeeds (selected range)
panels.description:
FOLLOWS THE TIME PICKER. Of the regenerations that ended in a working brief, how many tries into that day's sequence they were. Bar 1 is briefs that worked first time; bar 2 is briefs that needed a second go, and so on.

GOOD: almost everything in bar 1 - when people re-run a brief it works immediately.
BAD: weight in bars 2, 3 and 4+ - people are having to try repeatedly to get a brief out of the system, which is both a reliability problem and a compute bill, since every failed try is a full agent run that produced nothing.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM 'Failures nobody retried' ABOVE: that panel measures HARM - people who gave up or were never told and ended the day with nothing. This one measures EFFORT - what it cost the people who persisted. A feature can look fine here and still be failing badly there, because everyone counted in this chart eventually succeeded.

COUNTS SUCCESSES ONLY. Failed attempts are not in these bars; they are in the two panels above. The attempt number is the position in that day's regeneration sequence, capped at '4+'.

STARTS FROM THE FIRST GENERATION AFTER THIS SHIPPED. The attempt label was added on 2026-08-24, so runs recorded before that carry no attempt and are excluded from these bars entirely. Expect the chart to be empty at first, and do not read that as 'nothing succeeds'.

Both counters reset when the backend restarts, and increase() extrapolates to the window edges, so treat these as close estimates rather than exact tallies - a value of 4.7 failures means about five.
